```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 100)
```

```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
```

Every FCA or allocation analysis needs three aligned inputs: demand counts at
origins, supply at facilities, and travel between them. This guide prepares
them from the open Cornwall GP data bundled with spax and shows three common
problems: facility IDs that must match, unknown travel times, and demand that
arrives as small-area totals rather than a grid. Everything runs offline.

```{r data}
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")       # WorldPop 2020 residents
travel <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif") # minutes, one layer per practice
gp <- st_drop_geometry(cornwall_gp)
c(practices = nrow(gp), travel_layers = nlyr(travel),
  small_areas = nrow(cornwall_lsoa))
```

## Match facilities by ID, not by order

Each travel layer is named with the practice's NHS code, the same code as
`cornwall_gp$practice`. Check that the two sets agree before any calculation.

```{r ids}
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(gp$practice), setequal(names(travel), gp$practice))
head(names(travel))
```

When supply is a data frame, `spax_e2sfca()` and `spax_2sfca()` match its rows
to the travel layers through `id_col`, so the row order does not matter.

```{r id-order}
fit <- function(supply) {
  spax_e2sfca(pop, supply, travel,
    decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
    id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")$accessibility
}
shuffled <- arrange(gp, desc(practice))
all.equal(values(fit(gp)), values(fit(shuffled)))
```

A named supply vector is also matched by name, but an unnamed vector or a
matrix is used in layer order: then keeping the order right is your job. The
number of supply rows must equal the number of travel layers. Dropping a
facility from one input and not the other stops with an error:

```{r id-mismatch}
mainland_layers <- travel[[gp$practice[!gp$scilly]]]
tryCatch(spax_e2sfca(pop, gp, mainland_layers,
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
  id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"),
  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

## Decide what unknown travel means

Travel is `NA` where a cell is unpopulated, where there is no road connection
and for journeys over 180 minutes. In Cornwall the gaps come from the Isles of
Scilly: their practice cannot be reached by road from the mainland, mainland
practices cannot be reached from the islands, and some cells on the smaller
islands reach no practice at all.

```{r travel-na}
missing_cells <- global(is.na(travel), "sum")[[1]]
table(scilly_practice = gp$scilly, missing_cells)
road_scilly <- !is.na(values(travel[["L82017"]], mat = FALSE))
road_mainland <- !is.na(values(travel[[1]], mat = FALSE))
residents <- values(pop, mat = FALSE)
round(c(to_mainland = sum(residents[road_mainland]),
  to_scilly_practice = sum(residents[road_scilly]),
  no_road_link = sum(residents[!road_mainland & !road_scilly], na.rm = TRUE)))
```

The FCA functions drop unknown weights from their sums (`gather_weighted()`
defaults to `na.rm = TRUE`), so an `NA` travel time acts like "no access". Run
on all 55 practices, the islands become a separate system with one practice
and few residents, so their index is far above the mainland's. The residents
with no route drop out of that practice's demand and get no index at all.

```{r scilly-effect}
with_scilly <- 1000 * values(fit(gp), mat = FALSE)
round(c(mainland_median = median(with_scilly[road_mainland]),
  scilly_median = median(with_scilly[road_scilly])), 2)
```

The islands do have access, by boat and air, which the road-based travel times
do not represent. Rather than read these numbers as access, the FCA guides
model **mainland Cornwall only**: the 54 mainland practices and the cells with
a travel time to every one of them.

```{r mainland}
gp <- filter(gp, !scilly)
travel <- travel[[gp$practice]]
pop_mainland <- trim(mask(pop, sum(travel)))
travel <- crop(travel, pop_mainland)
stopifnot(compareGeom(pop_mainland, travel),
  identical(names(travel), gp$practice),
  !anyNA(values(travel)[!is.na(values(pop_mainland)), ]))
round(global(pop_mainland, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]])
```

`sum(travel)` is `NA` wherever any layer is `NA`, so the mask keeps exactly the
cells with complete travel. The check confirms that no populated cell has
unknown travel left.

## Turn small-area counts into a demand grid

Demand often comes as totals for administrative areas. `cornwall_lsoa` holds
ONS mid-2024 population estimates for the 337 small areas (LSOAs). To use them
on the grid, each area's total must be spread over its cells. Spreading it
uniformly would ignore where people live inside the area, so we use the
WorldPop grid as a pattern: `transform_pmf()` turns it into shares that sum to
1, and `transform_demand()` rescales those shares so that each area keeps its
own total.

```{r lsoa-too-small}
areas <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_transform(crs(pop)) |>
  vect()
pattern <- transform_pmf(pop)
lsoa_grid <- withCallingHandlers(
  transform_demand(areas, value_col = "pop", pmf = pattern, density = TRUE),
  warning = function(w) {
    message("Warning: ", conditionMessage(w))
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  })
```

The grid cells are about 1 km across, and many town LSOAs are smaller than
that: an area whose polygon contains no cell centre cannot receive its count,
and the function warns rather than silently losing people. The fix is to use
larger areas or a finer grid. Here we merge LSOAs into their middle-layer areas
(MSOAs): an LSOA name ends in a letter, and dropping it gives the MSOA name.

```{r msoa}
areas$msoa <- sub("[A-Z]$", "", areas$name)
msoa <- aggregate(areas, by = "msoa", fun = "sum")
ons <- transform_demand(msoa, value_col = "sum_pop", pmf = pattern,
  density = TRUE, full_output = TRUE)
c(areas = nrow(msoa), ons_total = sum(msoa$sum_pop),
  grid_total = round(global(ons$surface, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]))
signif(max(abs(ons$totals$original - ons$totals$redistributed)), 2)
```

All 73 areas keep their totals: the largest error is a fraction of a person.
The new grid has the ONS counts with the WorldPop pattern inside each area. The
two sources differ in date and method, so the ratio between them varies by
area. The map caps the colour scale at 0.5 and 1.5.

```{r ratio-map}
ratio <- crop(ons$surface / pop, msoa)
by_area <- extract(ratio, msoa, fun = median, na.rm = TRUE)[, 2]
round(summary(by_area), 2)
plot(clamp(ratio, 0.5, 1.5), axes = FALSE, range = c(0.5, 1.5),
  col = hcl.colors(50, "Blue-Red 3"),
  main = "ONS mid-2024 / WorldPop 2020 residents per cell")
lines(msoa, lwd = 0.3, col = "grey40")
```

In most areas the ONS estimate is higher, and in one it is more than three
times the WorldPop count. Decide which
source matches your question and say which you used; do not mix them within
one analysis. The other FCA guides use the WorldPop grid directly.

Two more cautions. If a source raster is a density (people per square
kilometre), multiply it by `terra::cellSize()` in the same area unit before use:
summing densities does not conserve counts, and longitude-latitude cells are
not all the same size. And `rasterize_demand()` does a different job: it
reweights a prior pattern by an area **rate** and returns shares, not counts
that respect area totals. For example, the share of residents aged 65 and over:

```{r rate}
msoa$share_65 <- msoa$sum_pop_65p / msoa$sum_pop
older <- rasterize_demand(msoa, value_col = "share_65", prior = pattern)
older_counts <- older * sum(msoa$sum_pop_65p)
kept <- extract(older_counts, msoa, fun = sum, na.rm = TRUE)[, 2] /
  msoa$sum_pop_65p
round(quantile(kept, c(0, 0.5, 1)), 2)
```

The shape is plausible (population times the local 65+ share), but area totals
are not kept: some areas end up with well under or over their known count. For
counts, use `transform_demand()`.

## The same rules for allocation inputs

The experimental allocation workflow takes a numeric origin-by-facility matrix,
`cornwall_travel`, from small-area centroids to practices. Its preparation is
strict: unknown travel on an active origin is an error unless you declare a
policy.

```{r allocation-na}
demand <- setNames(cornwall_lsoa$registered, cornwall_lsoa$lsoa)
supply <- setNames(cornwall_gp$gp_fte_extg, cornwall_gp$practice)
tryCatch(prepare_allocation(demand, supply, cornwall_travel),
  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

`missing_travel = "legacy_zero"` would omit unknown pairs, as the FCA functions
do. Positive infinity declares a known absent link. Neither describes the
islands' boat and air links, so we keep the mainland, matching IDs by name:

```{r allocation-mainland}
mainland_area <- !cornwall_lsoa$scilly
inputs <- prepare_allocation(demand[mainland_area], supply[gp$practice],
  cornwall_travel[mainland_area, gp$practice],
  metadata = list(demand_units = "registered residents",
    supply_units = "GP FTE excluding GPs in training", travel_units = "minutes"))
class(inputs)
```

The unit declarations are recorded, not converted. See the [allocation
workflow](allocation-workflow.html) for what the prepared inputs feed into.
